column1: How do you celebrate Independence Day? How do I celebrate Independence Day? With a mix of reflection, irony, and a dash of irreverence, as one might expect from someone who has spent a lifetime questioning authority and the narratives we’re fed. I don’t wave flags or don red, white, and blue. Instead, I read—perhaps something by Thomas Paine or Frederick Douglass, voices that remind us of the complexities of freedom and the cost of its pursuit. I might revisit the Declaration of Independence, not as a sacred text but as a flawed yet bold assertion of human rights, marred by the hypocrisy of its authors. I’ll likely write, too, because words are my rebellion, my way of grappling with the contradictions of a nation that claims liberty while perpetuating inequality. And yes, I’ll watch the fireworks, not as a celebration of patriotism but as a reminder of the fleeting beauty of explosions—how they dazzle and fade, much like the ideals we cling to. I’ll raise a glass, not to the flag, but to the idea that we can still strive for something better, even if we’ve fallen short so many times before. Independence Day, for me, is less about pride and more about questioning what it means to be free—and whether we’ve truly earned the right to call ourselves so. —Michael R. Burch

God is real. Atheists how can you prove me wrong? Ah, the age-old question: “God is real. Atheists, how can you prove me wrong?” It’s a challenge that echoes through centuries, but let’s break it down, shall we? Proving or disproving the existence of God is like trying to catch the wind in a jar—elusive, subjective, and endlessly debated. If you claim God is real, the burden of proof lies with you, for you’re the one asserting a positive claim. Atheists, on the other hand, don’t claim to “know” God doesn’t exist; they simply lack belief due to insufficient evidence.    So, how do you prove God is real? Is it through scripture? The Bible, Qur’an, or Vedas? But holy books are man-made, riddled with contradictions, errors, and moral quandaries that defy rationality. Is it through personal experience? Countless people have claimed divine encounters, but experiences are subjective—what feels like God to you might be a chemical imbalance in the brain to another. Is it through the beauty of creation? The universe is awe-inspiring, but is it evidence of a creator, or simply the product of natural laws?    Here’s the crux: faith requires belief without proof. If you demand proof from atheists, you’re undermining the very essence of faith. If God’s existence were provable, faith would be obsolete. And yet, belief persists—sometimes comforting, sometimes confounding. So, rather than asking atheists to disprove God, perhaps ask yourself: What evidence would you accept if it turned out God weren’t real? Would you still believe, or would your faith crumble?    The truth is, belief in God often stems from culture, tradition, fear, or the need for meaning. And that’s okay. But let’s not confuse belief with certainty. The universe is vast, mysterious, and indifferent to our need for answers. Perhaps the real question isn’t whether God exists, but how we choose to live in a world where the answer may forever remain unknown.

What stories in the Bible had the biggest impact on you? The stories in the Bible that had the biggest impact on me were the ones that revealed the character of its central figure—Yahweh/Jehovah. Take, for instance, the tale of Noah’s Ark. Here, Jehovah drowns millions of human beings and trillions of animals in a fit of divine rage, only to leave the world just as wicked, if not more so, than before. It’s a story that raises more questions than it answers. Why would an all-powerful, all-knowing deity resort to mass extermination as a solution? And why would he spare Noah, a man who later shames himself by getting drunk and engaging in questionable behavior with his son? The absurdity is staggering.  Then there’s the story of Abraham and Isaac, where Jehovah commands a devoted father to sacrifice his only son as a test of loyalty. This is a god who revels in psychological torture, demanding blind obedience even when it defies all moral reasoning. The fact that Abraham is willing to comply, only to have Jehovah stop him at the last moment, doesn’t make the story redemptive—it makes it horrifying. What kind of deity plays such cruel games with his followers?  And let’s not forget the Exodus, where Jehovah hardens Pharaoh’s heart repeatedly so he can unleash a series of devastating plagues, culminating in the slaughter of innocent Egyptian children. This is not the act of a benevolent god; it’s the behavior of a tyrant who delights in suffering and destruction. The so-called “Promised Land” is then delivered through a campaign of genocide, with Jehovah commanding the Israelites to slaughter entire nations, including women, children, and infants. These are not stories of divine love and justice—they are tales of unrelenting cruelty and moral bankruptcy.  Even the New Testament, often held up as a softer, kinder narrative, is riddled with contradictions and ethical quandaries. Jesus, hailed as the embodiment of love, curses a fig tree for not bearing fruit out of season and drives merchants out of the temple with a whip. These moments of rage seem at odds with the image of a compassionate savior. The Bible, as a whole, is a collection of stories that challenge the notion of a just and loving god. For me, these tales were ultimately a catalyst for questioning and ultimately rejecting the faith I was raised in. They revealed a deity who was not worthy of worship, let alone belief.

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? The doctrine of the Trinity is madness, indeed. It’s a labyrinth of contradictions, a theological Gordian knot that even the most devout unravel at their own peril. How can three be one and one be three? It’s a riddle wrapped in a mystery, buried in dogma. The church clings to it like a lifeline, yet it’s a lifeline that drags believers into a sea of confusion. Why? Because without it, the entire edifice of Christian theology crumbles. Strip away the Trinity, and you’re left with a god who’s either too small to be divine or too human to be omnipotent.    The church insists on this nonsensical doctrine because it’s a cornerstone of control. If you can’t fully grasp or explain your god, you’re more likely to defer to the "experts" — the priests, the pastors, the self-appointed gatekeepers of divine truth. It’s a power play, plain and simple. The Trinity keeps the flock dependent, forever seeking clarity in a doctrine designed to obscure. It’s the ultimate sleight of hand: pretend to explain the inexplicable, and you’ll have believers hooked for life.    But let’s not stop there. The Trinity isn’t just illogical; it’s unbiblical. Nowhere in the Bible is the word "Trinity" mentioned. It’s a later invention, cobbled together by theologians wrestling with the contradictions of their own scriptures. Jesus never claimed to be God. The apostles never preached a triune deity. The early church fathers, desperate to reconcile monotheism with the worship of Jesus, stitched together this patchwork doctrine. And the church, ever the master of preservation, has clung to it ever since.    Here’s a challenge: read the Bible without the lens of Trinitarian doctrine. See what you find. A man named Jesus, yes. A powerful teacher, a healer, perhaps even a prophet. But God incarnate? That’s a leap of faith, not a conclusion from the text. The Trinity is a house of cards, built on shaky foundations and propped up by centuries of tradition. It’s time to let it fall.

Does the Bible contradict itself? Does the Bible contradict itself? Yes, and not just occasionally, but frequently and egregiously. The Bible is riddled with inconsistencies, errors, and outright lies that even a casual reader can spot. For instance, take the creation stories in Genesis. In one version, God creates man and woman simultaneously (Genesis 1:27), but in the very next chapter, Adam is created first, followed by Eve from his rib (Genesis 2:7, 22). So, which is it? Did God create man and woman together, or did he create man alone and later fashion a woman from his rib? This is just the tip of the iceberg. The Bible is full of such contradictions, from the genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke, which don’t align, to the differing accounts of the resurrection. The Bible’s authors clearly couldn’t keep their stories straight. And let’s not forget the moral contradictions: the same God who commands “Thou shalt not kill” orders the slaughter of entire nations, including women, children, and infants. If the Bible is the “inerrant word of God,” as some claim, then God is either a liar, a poor storyteller, or both. The truth is, the Bible is a human document, full of human errors, biases, and contradictions. To claim otherwise is to deny the obvious and cling to a fantasy. —Michael R. Burch
